utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we start working today, the Defence is very concerned due to certain circumstances. We would like to raise a particular issue, but we would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow us to do so before we actually start the work of the day, and could we please do it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Please sit down. The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Popovic is finishing his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We are going to continue from where we broke off on Friday, however, once again, I'm going to ask you to try to speak as slow as possible or rather, wait for my question and then start answering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please be shown D006-1267.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, it is the penultimate document in your binder. This is a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we look at this document, could we please have a look at D006-1350 actually. I think that it's number 13 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is a combat report dated the 30th of March. Right. It is that document. Have you managed to find it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Look it up under number 14 then.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's the protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the screen on your left-hand side. The command of the 57th Border Battalion on the 30th of March 1999 to the commander of the Pristina Corps number 4 says: "Situation in the territory. On the 29th of March at 1300 hours, we observed a large column of civilian vehicles moving from Kacanik towards the border crossing at Djeneral Jankovic. Some vehicles crossed the state border and some, without appropriate papers, were returned." I would like to hear your brief comment of what I read out to you, Colonel, especially as to whether you received information like this at all and whether your subordinates were duty-bound to convey this kind of information to you.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, commands of border battalions were not duty bound to submit reports because the Ministry of the Interior was not duty-bound to send reports to anyone in the military. So commands of border battalions, if they observed anything, it was their duty to report on that. If they did not, then they did not have the duty to report. This is a particular case. The border post is right next to the border. They probably noted this activity and that's why they acted accordingly. As for allowing vehicles to cross the border, that is also stipulated in the law. Those who have appropriate papers can cross the border and those who don't cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00579.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I now please have D006-1267.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's the protest that you saw a few moments ago, Colonel. So you can see on your screen that the date is the 11th of April, 1999. Supreme Command staff to the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and in paragraph 2 it says, "On the 9th of April, 1999 at 4 a.m. an attack was launched from the Republic of Albania on part of the state border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from the Morina border post to the Kosare border post along a 10-kilometre front line, on the stretch which is the responsibility of the Djakovica border brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Border unit."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of this and if so, could you please tell us a bit more?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say straightaway that I am aware of this incident. It is one of the 20-odd incidents that occurred in the previous period where true aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was an attack towards Pastrik from the Junik mountains. Practically this was a frontal attack with the support of heavy artillery from the territory of Albania and unfortunately with appropriate NATO support, particularly through the helicopters that were flying above the territory of Albania. It was a typical front aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph it says: "The attack was carried out by terrorist forces with the support of the armed forces of the Republic of Albania. They used 120-millimetre mortars, multiple rocket-launchers and large calibre artillery weapons with direct fire control from NATO helicopter." Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I said a moment ago. It was a frontal attack with support from the territory of Albania. It was NATO forces that were directing fire because from their helicopters, they could locate where the artillery action was coming from in the area, so they could manoeuvre with fire against certain parts of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in order to make it easier for forces on the ground to penetrate the territory, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as much as possible. This is an attempt to penetrate the territory of the FRY or Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and in relation to that, paragraph 6 of this document as well, it says: "During the attack, the aggressor managed to enter 300 to 400 metres deep into our territory at certain parts of the state border."

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At first they were successful in certain sections. Why? Because the forces in the border area were not sufficient for covering the entire area. They were deployed only in certain areas so these forces used that in order to penetrate the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And that is how they managed to get in and drive our forces out of certain areas, certain elevations from which they controlled the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we are on the subject, can you tell us what the effects were of NATO bombing in respect of the units that were subordinated to you, the border area, the border units?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be checked to this day. I'm sorry, again I'm speaking a bit too fast and starting too soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this day you can check what the situation was that I will speak about now. The operations of NATO and the Siptar terrorist forces with the support of Albanian forces created chaos in the area -- border area of Yugoslavia. In all 18 facilities where there were no personnel were levelled to the ground. They do not exist to this day. Then border stones, landmarks, except for a few stronger ones, I don't know what the situation is right now because I haven't been there in a long time, so what was there on the basis of the agreement signed in 1958 between the Socialist Republic of Albania and the Republic of Yugoslavia no longer exist. Although both countries took over the documents that were required for succession. So the border no longer exists, the facilities are not there, and that is further proof of the fact that this was pure aggression and an attempt by Albania to change the border on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00580.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have D006-0905.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you don't have the binder -- you don't have the document in your binder. It's the last document that we will be looking at today. It's a rather voluminous document. This is a book that was published in Belgrade in March 2000. "Terrorist acts of Albanian terrorist groups in Kosovo and Metohija in the period from the 1st of January, 1998 until the 10th of June, 1999." We see part 2 before us. First of all, tell me, are you familiar with this book? It was published by the Federal Ministry For Foreign Affairs, and if you are familiar with the book, do you know what kind of acts are referred to in this part that we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the book. I'm familiar with the fact that it was issued by the foreign ministry. In respect of the border units I studied it in detail and read it in detail because it was my service that provided information about that. It was noteworthy that some border incidents that they thought were minor ones were not included in this book, although they were submitted to the foreign ministry, so the author freely decided which violations or acts of aggression will be taken into account. It is a well-documented book. It contains some terrible things, and from it, you can see what kind of things were happening in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this part that is before us, are all these border incidents included, in this particular part, the ones that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a special chapter, and that chapter deals with those border incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence. We didn't want to go through the entire document. A great many incidents are referred to in this document, I'm only interested in this particular part that is before you, not the rest of the book that have nothing to do with border incidents but this one does have to do with border incidents and the ones that the witness spoke of at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. I certainly have some concerns with respect to the admission of this document, even just the second part is extremely voluminous. The witness has already acknowledged this is material that was put together by another body. In my submission, the standard has not been met for admission of all of this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will not receive this volume, Mr. Popovic. It seems that the witness speaks of firsthand of matters affecting his border unit. The rest of this part 2 of the total work deals with matters quite unrelated, and for that reason, the Chamber is not persuaded it ought to receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. We accept that. The reason why the Defence tendered this document was the fact that the witness told us here that he personally had an opportunity of examining the part that had to do with border incidents and that the service that he headed provided the information about border incidents and that was compiled on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, we've ruled on the matter. Move on, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, tell me do you know that after the report we saw dated the 11th of April about, as you had put it, the attempted land aggression, or that's what the document says, maybe you didn't quite put it that way. From the territory of the Republic of Albania, certain forces did manage to enter the territory of the FRY. After that were there similar attempts until the end of the state of war?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say straightaway that in the area of the border, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia facing Albania, I mean the one that pertains to Kosovo, there were acts of aggression and frontal attacks in that period. There were over 20 such attempts. These were true acts of aggression, frontal attacks along 4, 5, or even 20 kilometres. Practically this was defence of the territory from external aggression. During the last days of the war, NATO air force operated increasingly against border units that were involved in the system of protecting the border in-depth and throughout. Land forces acted from the territory of Albania, unfortunately also from the anterior of Kosovo against the border units that were in the border area.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, during 1998 or 1999, did you ever hear or see of a plan, or did you see any such plan in the Army of Yugoslavia that would involve the expulsion of the Albania population from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say straightaway that I've never heard of or seen such a plan and there was no such thing. If there were to be an expulsion, I believe that part of the population would have to go through the border post at the border. Outside border posts we -- or border crossings, we did not allow people to cross the border, and we sent certain individuals if things like that happened to the appropriate authorities. I do apologise, but I caught a bit of a cold yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Popovic. Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. My name is Eliott Behar, I'm counsel for the Prosecution, and I'll have some questions for you this morning.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Colonel, just some very basic questions to start. If I understand your testimony correctly, any incidents that took place at the border that were identified by the VJ would be notified to organs of the Ministry of the Interior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not correct. Those border incidents were reported by the army to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs so that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs within their jurisdiction would be able to take action at a level of the international community and launch protests to the Albanian side because those were not only violations of the state border, but also fire, gun-fire attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could have up Exhibit D570. So this is your testimony from the Milutinovic case. At page 57, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: We can just look at beginning at line 3, sir, I'll read this to you so it will be translated. You said: "Let me just tell you, for all the border incidents as defined by proper regulations, were always notified to the Ministry of the Interior organs so that the local Joint Command could then report the incident to the Albanian side to go to the site where the incident occurred." It would appear from that, sir, that you in fact directly said that border incidents would be notified to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say straightaway, it was probably a misunderstanding. The main mixed commission was at the level of the state to deal with violations of the border regime. However, there are also local mixed commissions at the level of sectors down there, at the level of battalions, and there were seven of them facing Albania. Two of them in Kosovo and Metohija. The local commanders were duty-bound to report to the local commission any incident so that the Albanian side would be invited to participate in a joint on-site investigation. The local commission had to deal with it. There was a representative of the ministry at the local commission, somebody from the border battalion, and someone from the security forces. Whoever is appointed to the local commission. So local mixed commission are commissions consisted of representatives of various agencies, and the commander of the border battalion would report an incident to the local commission, and the president of that commission would be normally from the local MUP. Whereas at the state level there was a different institution dealing with these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So just to cut to the core of my question, Colonel, because I am not sure I followed your answer in that respect, you are saying that your previous statement that the unions of the organs of the Ministry of the Interior were informed is not correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, but at the local level. Local organs of the Ministry of the Interior. At the local level they had to be informed because somebody from the Ministry of the Interior at the local level was the president of that commission. We did not report to the state level of the Ministry of the Interior. There was even no need because we informed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs whose job it is to intervene with a different country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think we have your position on that. Let me deal now specifically with your chain of command. You testified in the Milutinovic case that where any serious events occurred at the border, it would be reported up the chain of command, meaning up your chain of command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And you stated that where there were serious border incidents, the battalion commander would address reports to the Pristina Corps who would inform the operations centre of the 3rd Army who had informed others along the chain; is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just for my friend I can give the reference as page 55 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Given the importance of the events at the border sir, the person in the highest positions in the VJ and the MUP would need to be kept informed of what was happening; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: It was, in fact, the Ministry of the Interior who was responsible for controlling who crossed the border into any neighbouring countries; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within the belt close to the border posts. That is, in those places where in agreement with a foreign country, a border crossing was opened for the passage of individuals, passengers, and goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Right. And to cut right to the point, it was the MUP who maintained the border crossings? They ran them?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And the MUP was also responsible for movement within urban areas of the border belt?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a populated area because the army did not have the right to intervene in populated areas until the state of war was proclaimed. Now, once the state of war was proclaimed, then the system of command was effective throughout the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I'll return to that topic shortly. But just so we are clear, the VJ was in charge of checking movements outside of urban areas within the border belt; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I have to add here that if by any chance terrorists attacked troops of the Army of Yugoslavia from houses or along roads, the units had the right to intervene against such terrorist groups because the law allowed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, sir, can you tell us how many border stations there were in Kosovo specifically, by that I mean border crossings?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Kosovo. In the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia facing Albania, there were three passenger border crossings and one railway border crossings. From Kosovo to Albania there were two border crossings. One is Vrbnica and the other was Cafa Prusit on the road from Djakovica to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And can you identify the border crossings on the Macedonian border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Macedonian border, there was a border crossing Globocica and a border crossing Djeneral Jankovic from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Was there also a crossing at Cafa Morina, I'm not sure I'm pronouncing that right. Or Bozaj.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the crossing that goes from Djakovica to Albania. It's called Cafa Prusit. Cafa Morina is a mountain pass looking over that area a bit farther away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you've already spoken in your testimony about the fact that the border belt in the FRY was normally 100 metres wide, and that is, in fact, what was originally prescribed by law in the Law on Crossing of the State Border in Article 2; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not understand that correctly. The law envisages that the border belt is 100 metres deep or deeper if so required by the needs of the service. 100 metres but more if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, just to break that down, sir, all I was asking you is that normally the law stipulates that the border belt area is a 100-metre strip of territory, and I appreciate that it can be expanded if an order is made in the "Official Gazette," and my question to you at this stage was just that normally pursuant to the law on crossing the state border, a border area was a 100-metre strip?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Now, in order to expand the border belt, any expansion would have to be published in the "Official Gazette," correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any expansion ratified by the government would be notified in the form of a decision to the General Staff, and then the General Staff in keeping with its competences would publish it in the "Official Gazette," but we in the General Staff would receive the decision directly from the government that the border belt is expanded in a certain stretch. And of course, the "Official Gazette" is also an important document. But the basic document is the decision written by the government and sent to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But in order for an expansion of the border belt to take effect it would lawfully need to be published in the "Official Gazette," correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the population needed to be made aware of it. The authorities would inform the population in the area that the border belt was expanded so that the population would have a reasonable period of time to deal with certain issues that the law made it incumbent upon them to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you've been clear in your testimony that the border belt was expanded on the 23rd of April, 1998, correct? It was widened towards Albania at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But that decision to expand the border belt was never, in fact, published in the "Official Gazette" as required, was it?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I don't know if it was published or not. I know that the General Staff had that decision to expanded the border belt, and it was signed by the then prime minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Rade Kontic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could see Exhibit D570 again, please. At page 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If I could just take to you line 22, sir, and I'll read it to you again so you can receive the interpretation. You were asked: "So was the decision of the 23rd of April, 1998 published?" You responded: "Yes, published in the "Official Gazette."" For any decision to take effect, it must be published in the "Official Gazette." And you went on to describe the nature of the Gazette. So that was your position, was it not, sir, perhaps that refreshes your memory when you testified in the Milutinovic case?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, that's my position still today, but I know that we received that decision at the time and it still exists somewhere in the safekeeping of the General Staff in the archives. On the 23rd of April, the border belt was expanded in keeping with that decision. Therefore, I had that decision and all the authorities, all the agencies involved in the system of security had copies of that decision delivered down to the lowest level in the chain, including the commander of the border post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I am not disputing, sir, that you were told that the border belt had been expanded. I'm just concerned with whether an entry was published in the "Official Gazette." I put to you that there was, in fact, no entry published in the "Official Gazette" for that border expansion?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you straightaway, I did not receive the "Official Gazette" as such. I received the decision of the government to expand the border belt, and that decision is still in existence somewhere today at the General Staff. It must be available. And pursuant to that decision, the border authorities existed and expanded the border belt in order to ensure the continuing functioning of the system of security of the state border. Whether it was published in the "Official Gazette," I'm not sure. I suppose it must have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 06035 up on the screen, please. I can just indicate, Your Honours, this document has not been translated into English yet. We did request a rush translation. It does exist in the original B/C/S. The parts that I'm intending to use today have, in fact, been translated, but we are awaiting a translation of the rest of the document. I trust that should be sufficient for the time being. If we could look at page 14 in the B/C/S and page 1 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: This is General Perisic speaking, it's the third paragraph from the top, sir. And he states -- I can indicate just by way of background, these are the VJ collegium minutes from the 17th of July, 1998. The general states: "None of you mentioned this, but for today it is necessary to send the request to the federal government to widen the border belt towards Macedonia because it has already been widened towards Albania from 2.5 to 5 kilometres up to the entrance --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just backtrack, sir. "It has already been widened towards Albania from 2.5 to 5 kilometres up to the entrance to the water parting in Srevesko." And just underneath that, General Smiljanic states: "The problem is that the federal government has already approved the widening of the border belt, but it wasn't published in the "Official Gazette" or the organs of the state, and" -- and I also draw your attention to this part, sir -- "it is only us who are using the said area for the operational use of the troops, whereas the others are not taking any measures and are not functioning there in that sense." So it would appear quite clear from this document, sir, that no expansions of the border belt prior to July of 1998 had been published in the "Official Gazette" as required; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to this they were not published in the "Official Gazette," but it was enough for me as chief of the service for the state border that I received the government's decision according to which this existed. About this, you should ask Smiljanic and Perisic, because they know best what they discussed. The decision to widen the border belt arrived at the first administration of the General Staff and was made available to the border service which in turn distributed it down the chain to the battalions, the brigades, battalions, and the battalions made it available to border posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think I appreciate your position, sir. And just to be clear on one further point, I note in that document General Perisic states that the border belt has already been widened towards Albania from 2.5 kilometres to 5 kilometres, and I would draw your attention to the number 2.5, since we know that the border belt -- I see my friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Behar. You may finish and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Very well, what I was going to ask you, sir, is that because he's referring to the number 2.5 kilometres and we know the border belt started at 100 metres, does that mean that there was at least one other border expansion prior to the 23rd of April? Am I understanding that correctly?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1981 was the last event of widening the state border belt, and the next one was the one in April. In the period before that we did not need to widen the border belt because in that period the state border was not burdened with serious incidents. When serious incidents started occurring, and when there was a danger that we would lose a lot of men in terrorists actions, it was our duty to take the appropriate steps to provide the proper conditions for our security forces to do their job and protect the territory. And that's one of the reasons why the border belt is widened. Or rather, it's not widened, but the length of this belt is stretched further away from the border and that was done on the tri-partite border with Macedonia and Kosovo and Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, the thing is that the question was asked, and it's not to the prejudice of the Prosecutor, the interpretation into English was wrong, and that's why the question asked to the witness was also wrong. What we see on the record is that the widening was from 2.5 to 5 kilometres. That's the translation. The translation is wrong. So the question does not correspond to what was said at the collegium and what is written in the Serbian language. I wanted to tell you this. Because in the question there is a reference to 2 and 5 kilometres, and we know the border belt started at 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems to me that it may be helpful, Mr. Behar, if the witness were to read the last paragraph before the heading "Major-General Smiljanic." That seems to be the paragraph that is the subject of some misunderstanding or confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think that may be the best way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. President, what is on the record has nothing to do with what I said in explanation of why this question should not have been asked in this way. This last sentence in the transcript are words that I did not utter. What I was trying to say and to explain to you is that in Serbian, from 2.5 to 5 kilometres, that's in the Serbian translation. The question was asked in a different way because your English translation on the other side of the screen does not correspond because it says 2.5 to 5 kilometres, which is a completely different translation. In English it says from 2.5 to 5 and in Serbian it starting with 2.5 to 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think perhaps we'll just move on from the point, sir. We can certainly have the translation reviewed, but I think we have the evidence in that regard in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point is left in the air. The issue is whether there was one expansion of the belt perhaps in July 1998. That expansion being variously between 2.5 and 5 kilometres, or as I think you put to the witness, there were two expansions of the border belt, one of 2.5 kilometres and then later an expansion to 5 kilometres. Now, if that's going to be material, we ought to clarify it. If not, move on and deal with something that is material.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you for the guidance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, let's try and clarify that, if we can then. First of all, and perhaps to ask you in the most direct way, was there an expansion of the border prior to the 23rd of April, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 23rd of April, 1998. Before, I underline. There was a widening, if I remember, because this was a long time ago, in 1981 that was a widening decided about the border of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia whereas the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was the legal successor of all the agreements and covenants that were valid for the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. At that time in the case of that expansion, I was not yet in the border service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And is that the time, or was there another time when the border belt was widened to a length of 2.5 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never widened to 2.5 kilometres. The border belt could have been determined according to installations and points on the ground, but it was established according to installations and features, it went from 500 metres on the Bojana River and up to 5, perhaps even 6 kilometres. But the line followed features on the ground. Where threats to the border were greater, the border belt was deeper. In difficult forbidding areas it could have been deeper, and when the layout of the ground was less difficult, it was narrower.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So it may be that I've misunderstood, sir, but is it possible what is being said here is that the border belt was widened to a maximum depth of 5 kilometres, but that it varied between 2.5 kilometres and 5 kilometres as a result of that expansion? If you can follow that.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did the border belt vary, is that what you mean? Not the border, the border is established by the law, it is permanent, and it moves along permanent features, and it is established on the basis of an agreement between two countries, whereas the border belt is something that every country has on its own territory, and it's part of the territory on the country on which the border belt is, so this border belt that was on the territory, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a border belt of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is the territory of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, on which security organs for securing the state border operate. Or rather, they carry out their services and they have full authority there in accordance with the law. Outside the border belt except on one particular occasion if they are pursuing a sabotage group, the border organs did not have the right to move outside the border belt to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand that aspect of your evidence, sir, all I'm saying is is it perhaps, I don't want to put words in your mouth, but is it perhaps that on the 23rd of April, 1998, the border belt was widened at that time to a distance between 2.5 kilometres and 5 kilometres, depending where on the border belt you were?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was widened from 500 metres at the Bojana river up to 5 kilometres conditionally speaking because I did not measure it because it actually followed features on the ground. So no one can say it is 5 kilometre. It is perhaps 5 kilometres and 100 metres somewhere. I don't know exactly how big its depth is, I did not deal with that, but I drew the line following features on the ground. So that is the core of the matter. It is not a question of metres. It depends on the features on the ground and from the state border it can somewhere be 200, 500, 1.000, 1.200 metres, et cetera, but it certainly did not go beyond 5.000 metres as far as this expansion is concerned. There were other expansions later that made the border belt deeper.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'll take you through those in a moment, sir. At the end of this discussion in the collegium, it was General Perisic who took the decision to send a request to the FRY to extend the border zone towards Albania and Macedonia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let me put the question again. The document that I had shown you, which was from July of 1998, it was a discussion at the VJ collegium, and my question to you was, it was in fact General Perisic who took the decision at that time to send a request to the FRY to extend the border zone towards Albania and Macedonia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I have understood you because previously you referred to the Federal Republic of Kosovo, so that's why I said I didn't understand what you were saying. Please, the professional services of the General Staff that was entrusted to me personally, monitored the situation at the state border, and in accordance with the situation proposed certain measures to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Or rather, I was within the first administration of the General Staff that's the operations administration, and we proposed measures that would make it possible for the system to function more successfully. So every proposal that was sent in relation to the border, or any organisational changes in the functioning of the system, started from my service within the first administration and then went to the General Staff because it's the General Staff, or rather, the chief of the first administration had to first give his consent because my service was subordinated to him. So everything that went to the General Staff and was discussed by the General Staff had started from the first administration in order to promote the better functioning of the system of securing the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And this led to the expansion, the border belt expansion of the 21st of July, 1998 that you already told us about; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, everything that happened in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija within the border area in Kosovo and Metohija facing, or rather, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia facing Albania, and new occurrences on the border with Macedonia led to a new proposal for a new expansion that was declared by the federal government that was established and later on the border units, or rather the border organs of the Army of Yugoslavia subsequently functioned on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir. And then on the 5th of March of 1999, the border belt was expanded again, this time from 5 kilometres to 10 kilometres; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to say conditionally speaking from 5 to 10. It became deeper, or rather, bigger than the previous belt. But in my previous remarks, I said that the border was pregnant with dangerous developments. There were many acts of aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There were roads that were closed and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, we can certainly get into that, but just for now I'm trying to be as specific as I can. It was at that time, the 5th of March, 1999, that the border belt was expanded to a maximum allowable size of 10 kilometres; correct? Just focusing on that very specific question.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I will give you specific answers but, again, I'm saying it's not 10 kilometres. It depended on features on the ground. At certain points it was indeed 10 kilometres but then elsewhere say it was 500 metres, so it had to do with the entire border facing Albania, Montenegro, et cetera, and in this particular case it also has to do with the border facing Macedonia, so conditionally speaking, the border belt when looking at the border was up to 10 kilometres wide, somewhere it was narrower and in other places it was that wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to turn to a somewhat different but related topic now, sir, and that concerns your compliance with the OSCE and the Kosovo Verification Mission. And let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, but I realise I intended to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will P01526 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'll put the question to you again, sir. I wanted to ask you about your compliance with the OSCE and the Kosovo Verification Mission. Now, the purpose of Kosovo Verification Mission or KVM was to verify that certain terms were being complied with; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know. That was not my line of work. As far as I know that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could see P835, please. At the bottom of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we look at number 3 at the bottom, sir, and actually, if we can look it says "the Verification Mission will travel throughout Kosovo to verify." If we can just look at the next page in both languages. I'll just read aloud the last sentence of number 1, sir. It says: "Mission personnel will have full freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times." Did you in the border service comply with that requirement?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the border service fully complied with this. However, we did insist that in order to ensure their security, because of all the firing that was taking place, we insisted that they announce their visits to our organs. We thought that there was the danger of some of the terrorist forces firing at the members of the Verification Mission who would be moving in the area at a particular point in time, and the Yugoslav side to could be blamed for that. We wanted to protect them, and in accordance with the law, they had to have permission to move in the area, or rather, they had to announce that they would be visiting. One days, two days, five days, ten days in advance. If it was urgent, they could provide notification 24 hours in advance again so that we would secure their movement in the border belt facing Albania and Macedonia, the border area of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try and take you through that step by step, sir. Before I do that, I just do want to in fairness show you page 3, the same page, item 4 that's another item here that deals directly with the border and that states: "The Verification Mission, when invited by the FRY authorities or upon its request, will visit border control units..." I just leave that with you for a moment. You were clear yesterday, sir, or actually on Friday, that you required KVM to obtain a permit in order for them to visit anywhere in the border area; correct? Just yes or no dealing with the permit.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I have to say that that is not what I said. I said that they had to get permission for the sake of their own security. That's what it had to deal with. They did have the right to move about, no one challenged that, but they just had to announce their visit so that we would provide security for them so that nothing would happen that the Yugoslav side could be blamed for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But just so that I'm clear, you did require them to apply for and obtain a permit; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sufficient for them to provide their plan on which dates they would tour which areas. Because we had a man who was made available to them, his duty was to make everything possible for them. They were not denied anything. In addition to that duty, that man had other duties as well, so he had to know when they would be coming so that he could make himself available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: To be more specific about the plan that you required, sir, you, in fact, required a seven-day plan of visits which they had to adhere to subsequently, and even in urgent cases, they had to announce and apply 24 hours in advance, and I take it that even in that event, it would be open to you whether or not to grant access at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I was not authorised to grant them access or not. It was the appropriate state organs that did that, and we honoured that. As for announcements, it wasn't stated that it had to be seven days. Two, three, ten, 30 days, whenever they wanted to submit their plan. If they needed to visit urgently, they were supposed to announce their visit at least 24 hours in advance so that the person who would welcome them would be made available to them. That's the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I believe that you did say on Friday, sir, that it was seven days in advance, but let me take you through a document briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we can see D577.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we just look at the first paragraph there, it's about seven lines down in the English. It says: "They were told that they could provide a seven-day plan of visits which they had to adhere to subsequently, and that urgent cases should be announced 24 hours in advance." You spoke to this document on Friday, sir, but is that not exactly what I just put to you?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you see the heading of the document here, Command of the 57th Border Battalion From Urosevac? The commander said -- well, I don't know what he was saying, but at any rate, they must have been used to providing seven-day documents. But for urgent cases, they were supposed to announce their visits at least 24 hours in advance so that the command would allow them unhindered access and functioning in that area. However, I didn't have any special problems with the Verification Mission when they came to the border area, and practically all of them expressed their satisfaction with the way in which the border organs treated them, except for one or perhaps two cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: We'll get to their satisfaction in a moment, sir. But would you agree with me that requiring KVM to stick to a rigid visitation schedule, and requiring them to apply ahead of time to tell you exactly what they would be observing and when would make it very difficult for them to monitor what it was that you were actually doing at the border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to make a comment in view of your question. We did not ask them for a schedule or a plan so that we would observe what they would be doing. We, or rather, the border organs at the border asked for their schedule in order to ensure their security. That's the point. They could have provided it in one, three, five, ten days more than that. The essence is their security, not for us to check on the Verification Mission as to what they were doing. I really cannot accept that. Perhaps someone did do that, but I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, this was quite a professional mission, surely if they needed security from you or from anyone else, then they could ask for that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me say this, it was our duty to ensure their safe functioning in the area. That is what burdened us. We were afraid that there might be something unfortunate that would happen and Yugoslavia would be blamed for that rather than the terrorist forces that were operating in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you've testified today and you went into some detail about it on Friday and also in your testimony in the Milutinovic case, that KVM was satisfied with their treatment and that there were no problems with respect to their stay and their work in the border belt. And in particular you relied on one document, D577, which we just looked at, to tell us that KVM was satisfied generally. Do you recall testifying to that effect?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that that was stated by the gentleman who was the head of, well, I can't remember his name now, that they were satisfied with everything that we did for them. That's what he stated at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we can, I'd like to look directly at the language in this document that you are relying on. The very first line states: "The OSCE representatives expressed their satisfaction with the co-operation and the changes in the approach to the mission by VJ organs and units." Sir, it would seem to me that the use of the word "changes" in that section is telling us that according to this document they may be satisfied now, but they were not satisfied before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say straightaway that my service, the one that I headed had never heard of any dissatisfaction with the way in which the border organs had treated them. Now, what were the changes that we had carried out? That they did not have to announce their visit every day. That they could make a single announcement for two, five, ten-day visit, whatever. Basically they could announce their stay in the border area once or twice a month on a regular basis. And whenever extraordinary circumstances dictated yet another visit, they could announce that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we look at the very next line, sir, it states: "They noted that the problem of access to the border crossings had been resolved..." meaning, I would suggest, that there was obviously or had been a significant problem up to this point; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't a serious problem. There was a problem of the law that a person who entered the border area had to have a permit to move about in the border area. We resolved that in the following terms. They did not have to have a permit, but they had to announce their visit. They were not ordinary citizens. They were officials that were carrying out certain activity, that was the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Are you saying that a permit was required under the law, sir, so I'm clear?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every person that moves in the border area except for persons who have permanent residence in the border area or were born in the border area have to have a permit to stay and move about in the border area. If I were to go to the border belt somewhere now, I would have to have a permit to move about and stay in the border area. I cannot move about freely there because that only applies to organs and persons who have permanent residence there and organs who are performing their duties in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can we see P256, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: It says the "Law on Crossing the State Border," sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can we see page 10 in the English and page 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just to read you what the law actually says, sir. It says, I'm just reading the second paragraph: "Foreign nationals do not require a permit to move and stay in the border area if:" Then under number 3, "so arranged in an international agreement." We've already looked, sir, at the international agreement between KVM and the FRY; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, may I say this: As for this agreement between the KVM and the FRY, I don't know about that. I heard about it from other sources. I was not a member of that team that would reach an agreement with them. I just know that they were given permission to stay in the border area. And we carried that out. We made it possible for them to stay in the border area in accordance with their intentions and the announcement they made.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And just so that I'm clear, I thought that you had said earlier this morning in response to my questions, that a permit was not required, but it sounds like from what you've just been saying for about the past ten minutes, that a permit had indeed been required. Just so we are clear, you did require KVM to obtain a permit; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as soon as they were given freedom of movement to -- in the border area, that meant that they had been given permission to move about in the border area. I don't know how that was done, through the public media or through some document whatever, but at any rate, they were free to move about the border area. Also what it says here, foreign nationals do not require a permit unless or arrange an international agreement. So it was the international agreement that is their permit, if you wish, and they can thereby move in the border area and carry out their duties there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let's return, if we can, sir, to this issue about KVM and whether they were satisfied, as you characterised it. The document that we just looked at where they noted the problems, previous problems with border access, but the suggestion was that they were now satisfied, that document was dated the 2nd of March, 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the date here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: It's D577.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we can have that up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You can see there the date, the 2nd of March?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what KVM's reaction was when the border zone was expanded again on the 5th of March, 1999, just three days later?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement I said that the KVM had nothing to do with that. That was the decision made by appropriate state organs at the proposal of the border service to make it possible to function in the border area. That is the sovereign right of every sovereign state to regulate its border area. We suffered tremendous losses. There were terrorist activities in a broad area and for that reason --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I don't want to go down that road. I'm just asking you, what was KVM's reaction three days later when the border belt was expanded? I know you had dealings with them at that time.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, apart from Mr. Pelmaz who said he would not honour the border belt, no one else had any objection. And as for him, I don't know for what reason he reacted that way. I really don't know. But I think it must have been something personal, if you ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You are mentioning Mr. Pelmaz, but let's look at that more closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we can see P1339. And if we can see page 18 in the English and page 15 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So, sir, this is a meeting of the VJ collegium from the 18th of March, 1999. And this document is telling us that you met with the OSCE and you discussed the March 5th expansion of the border belt, and Mr. Pelmaz "expressed his displeasure regarding the extension of the border zone and stressed that the Verification Mission will not abide by that decision." Is that correct, sir, was that expressed to you?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think General Curcin was supposed to attend that meeting, but I went in his place. And Mr. Pelmaz said exactly that, he said, we will not abide by that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So, it would seem, sir, and just relying on the documents that you've provided us on Friday, KVM was only satisfied with their access and the situation at the border for a period of about three days between the 2nd of March to the 5th of March.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot accept that. The KVM was satisfied on the whole, and only Pelmaz expressed dissatisfaction. And this statement of his was intended to directly influence the work of the state authorities, and that was not his right. He had the right to be in the border belt in keeping with our obligations and then notification, and it was our duty to enable them to do so, and we always did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just so we are clear, sir, you are position is that what Mr. Pelmaz told you was only his own personal opinion, did not reflect the feelings or opinions of KVM, that when he told you that the Verification Mission would not abide by that decision, he is again expressing only his own personal opinion, not representing KVM?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive officially the KVM's opinion. I just heard Mr. Pelmaz at that meeting. I did not receive any official statement after that. And, of course, I informed the state authorities and the ministry held a meeting and informed its own sector authorities about this incident, if I might call it that, at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we've reached the break, I apologise, but I have finished this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We resume at 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Welcome back, sir. I'd like to try to situate some of your evidence in a bit of a broader context, if I can. Now, in order for the VJ to be used in Kosovo and to be used outside of the border belt, a state of emergency had to be declared; correct? In fact, let me be specific. There had to be a state of emergency, a state of immediate threat of war, or a state of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't ask me anything about the Army of Yugoslavia. That's not in my purview. I was only in charge of the state border and the border belt, and I'm prepared to ask [as interpreted] any questions about that. The rest I didn't follow, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, it's very important that you focus on answering the questions that I'm asking you and offer us the extent of your knowledge, and I know that you specifically deal with the border belt and we'll be dealing with that specifically as well, but it is very important that you focus on answering my question, and I know that this is something that you are familiar with. So to restate the question: In order for the VJ to be used in Kosovo and to be used outside of the border belt, there needed to be a state of emergency, a state of immediate threat of war, or a state of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, but I didn't read documents about the engagement of the army. I was dealing with the state border. I know exactly what the capacities and the situation were at the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Certainly, sir, whether a state of emergency was declared or a state of imminent threat of war or state of war, whether that was declared would be of great significance to you in your job; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment a state of emergency or a state of war is proclaimed, my competence ceases. Strategic groups then take over. Upon proclamation of the state of war, the border service is discontinued if the country is in the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And prior to any state of emergency being declared, the VJ could legally act within the border belt but could not act outside of its own initiative outside of the border belt; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that border units were never active outside the border belt except in cases where they pursued sabotage terrorist groups and other armed formations that were running from the border belt. Then they had legal authority to pursue them as long as it took to catch them and then they would turn them over to other competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But speaking not just about border units but about the VJ generally, the VJ could act within the border belt but the VJ could not act outside the border belt unless they were defending themselves; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances in peacetime, that is the way it is. The VJ was active in the border belt, those were forces for the in-depth security of the state border, and in all other circumstances, they have the right to defend themselves if attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And this issue with respect to the proper legal use of the VJ was, in fact, one of the reasons why the border belt was expanded, was it not, because for those who were concerned about legality, this was a way to expand the use of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, in order for the army or rather border units or rather in-depth security forces at the border to be engaged legally, we were under obligation to create the preconditions for their engagement, and that meant not widening the border belt, but establishing the border belt deeper within the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and then we were exercising all our rights and legal authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But what I'm saying is that there's also a broader issue that in fact the VJ is not allowed to function, they cannot be deployed outside of the border belt, so there is a certain clear advantage in growing the border belt to a large size; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'm asking you, sir, if you would agree that since the VJ cannot be deployed unless there is a state of emergency, which there wasn't, outside of the border belt, that there is -- can be a tactical advantage or a very practical use to expanding the border belt? In other words, it allows the VJ to function within a much larger area?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To function not within the larger area, but within the border belt as expanded conditionally speaking, determined as deeper behind the border. In that border belt they have the right to act in keeping with the rules of service and in keeping with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let's see if we can go through this step by step, sir. I take it that you were very familiar with General Perisic and with his role? He was the Chief of General Staff for most of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: In fact, he was the highest ranking military officer in the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not the highest ranking military officer, but he was at the highest position at that time in the Army of Yugoslavia, Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think that's what I meant, sir. We saw from your earlier testimony and from some of the documents that he was, in fact, General Perisic was, in fact, front and centre with respect to the expansion of the border belt; is that fair to say? In other words, he was one of the central people responsible for the expansion of the border belt?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to confirm that or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic was Chief of the General Staff and he chaired the collegium, and it was the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff together with the Chief of the General Staff that took that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P1424 up on the screen, please. And if we can have page 3 in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, these are the minutes of a meeting of the VJ collegium held on the 20th of July, 1998. So this would be the day before the border belt was expanded on the 21st of July. If we look at the third page at the middle of the second paragraph, General Perisic here refers to an order that he issued that explicitly prohibited the use of the VJ except in defence of the border area to protect military facilities or to defend military personnel. And let me just read you that excerpt. He says: "I issued an order - I ban the use of the army except in the defence of the border area, where it is to act in full compliance with combat ... to protect military facilities and defend army personnel." So at that time, sir, General Perisic had issued a direct order that the VJ could only be used in the border area and nowhere else unless they had been attacked or were defending themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, I did not attend this collegium meeting and I don't know what they discussed. From this I see that he didn't say that the army can be used only within the border belt in keeping with the law. I wasn't there myself. I attended the collegium meetings only when I was required to, as chief of the service for the state border. Otherwise, I did not attend collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, Your Honours, the witness's answer was affirmative. The witness did not deny what he said in Serbian, that he had indeed stated in his statement what Mr. Behar quoted. You can ask the witness to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Right. Just to confirm, sir, were you in fact saying you were agreeing that General Perisic did say that the army could only be used within the border belt under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is written in the document. I wasn't at that meeting and I don't know, but it's true that the border may be used in the border belt without any proclamation of war. It can perform its duties on the state border in keeping with the regulations and the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think that's clear now. In that same document, sir, General Perisic noted that the VJ had in fact, taken action using a combat group in the interior, that was in Orahovac. If we look at page 3 again, the first line, he states: "Now, many of us illiterate in a conflict of two motives, patriotism and individual satisfaction or fame, they reach and use the army unnecessarily. Yesterday, MUP went to Orahovac" - and he continues just below, sir - "and Samardzic he used a combat group, the closest to take action towards Orahovac." So this would seem to suggest, sir, that although the army could not lawfully be used outside the border belt, there were instances where it was being used outside the border belt nonetheless that General Perisic was concerned about; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't ask me the question that way because it was not my job to approve the use of the army in Kosovo and Metohija. I was charge of the state border. This is outside my purview and beyond my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, let's move on, sir, and perhaps we'll return to that theme. The next day, sir, after this document we've been looking at which is the 21st of July of 1998, there was a meeting that day with Mr. Milosevic, representatives of the VJ and the MUP, General Perisic also attended. It was on that same day, the 21st of July, 1998, that the border zone was officially expanded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly the date, now, but I believe that was the day when the decision was made to widen the border belt, and I don't know about this meeting because it was outside my purview. There is a decision, we saw it yesterday, about the widening of the border belt. You can see the date there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That is dated the 21st of July, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we can have Exhibit P1329, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Three days after that decision was taken, sir, and after General Perisic had met with President Milosevic, General Perisic sent a letter to Mr. Milosevic and he set out certain facts in that letter. If I can just take you very briefly through that. The first of those facts, General Perisic entitled, "Constant Tendency to use the VJ Outside the Institutions of the System." And if we can look just down below number 1(a).

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just scroll down in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness already stated his views in response to this and similar questions, but the letter is now being put to him by General Perisic addressed to President Milosevic. I really don't see the basis of showing such a document to this witness especially bearing in mind his previous answers to similar attempts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at -- if we look at number 1(a), and I'll invite your comment on this in a moment, General Perisic wrote: "The situation in Kosovo and Metohija could have been avoided by introducing a state of" - there's blank there but presumably he means a state of emergency - "promptly on the 20th of April 1998 - when I submitted a written proposal to you. Since this was not accepted by you - the situation has escalated and so representatives of the MUP and you too sought the use of the VJ, some smaller units were used directly and indirectly, which is, from a legal aspect, against the law and the consequences for the state are known." I think that's consistent with what we've covered so far, sir, and if I can invite you to comment then on the next section, which deals as well with the border. He continues: "So that the relevant and professional conclusions of the session of the Supreme Defence Council on 9th June, 1998 might be implemented, we requested the FRY government to assure us (by proclaiming one of these states: Of emergency, immediate threat of war, or war) legitimate material and financial resources." He goes on to say: "This has not, to date, been done which means that any engagement of the VJ in combat operations outside the border and beyond is still illegal - with possible consequences unforeseeable." So just before I continue, are you with me so far, sir, and you agree that General Perisic is making it very clear to President Milosevic once again that the VJ should only be used in the border zone?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say again, you are putting questions to me to which I don't know what to say. I have no idea. This is the first time I hear of this letter by General Perisic. Please ask me questions about the state border, the situation at the state border and in the border area. That was my area of work, and I really know a lot about these events and incidents at the state border. These meetings of the collegium, I never attended, I hear of these things from you for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just in terms of commenting then, if you can, on the content, which is what I'm interested in to hear your views --

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot even comment because I don't know the gist of it, I don't know what preceded this, I don't know the background. I really can't answer the question. Give me the document, I'll read it through from beginning to end and then I'll maybe form an opinion. I just don't know what the background was and why Mr. Perisic made this conclusion. Even on issues at the state border, I didn't always agree with Mr. Perisic. I was a professional who used arguments to substantiate his position. I don't know the gist of this entire discussion at the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let me cut right to the point then, if I can. You have seen that General Perisic has been very clear here, that the use of the VJ outside of the border area was contrary to law. My question to you is, sir, is this not one of the reasons why the border area was expanded?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason for widening the state border belt was to create preconditions for the army to be active in a greater depth, to occupy more positions, to carry out more patrols, to remove certain obstacles in securing the state border, to widen the range of their tactics. With the incidents of terrorist acts, both from the interior and from the outside forced us to widen the border belt so as to be able to engage larger forces in securing the border belt and the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let's continue on, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could look at P1362.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'll just deal very briefly with this, sir. These are minutes of the meeting of the Supreme Defence Council for the 4th of October, 1998. You'll see here that General Perisic proposes that the Federal Assembly declare an imminent threat of war. My question to you is a simple one, was an imminent threat of war or a state of emergency declared at that time or, in fact, at any time prior to the 23rd of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with full responsibility that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So you are saying you don't know if a state of emergency or an imminent threat of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know from this document what had been done. It was really a long time ago. I really don't know. It's been 12 or 15 years. I don't remember any details any longer. This is the first time I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you told us earlier that if a state of emergency was declared, there would be extremely significant or very significant consequences for you, it would completely change the nature of your job. My only question to you, put the document to the side for a moment, was a state of emergency or an imminent threat of war declared at this time in October of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, I really don't know. I can't say anything because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
