utterances.text: Well, did you continue functioning in your job as you normally would, sir, because if I understood correctly, you told us that earlier today if a state of emergency was declared, then you would, in fact, cease to operate as you had been operating?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, all the way up to the proclamation of the state of war, the state border operated as a system within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. From the moment when the state of war was proclaimed, the border units became part of operations units that protected the territory from outside aggression, and that is when my function in that part of the state border ceased. Under all other circumstances, we continued to monitor the situation because there was no frontal engagement of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Right. And there was no state of war declared at that time or imminent state of war, or a state of emergency? None of those things were done?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Having raised these concerns, and we've looked at a number of them here, sir, General Perisic was in fact replaced as the Chief of the General Staff; correct? That's something you would have been certainly aware of having attended all of these meetings, or a number of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know why General Perisic was replaced. I don't know the reasons because that was not within my purview. I didn't attend those meetings at the collegium, and ex officio, I couldn't attend, I couldn't be privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That's fine, I'm not asking you that. I'm just asking you to confirm that he was indeed replaced; correct? In fact, he was replaced on the 24th of November 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was replaced or simply someone took his place for official reasons, to meet the needs of the service. Just because I was sent by the army at some point to occupy different duties. I don't know what happened with Perisic. Maybe he was replaced, but maybe by the nature of the service, he was needed elsewhere. Maybe he was replaced for other reasons. Maybe he didn't meet the expectations, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think you've confirmed that he was replaced. He was in fact replaced by General Ojdanic, sir, and he was transferred to a post advisor to the federal government on defence issues. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I didn't say that Mr. Perisic had been replaced. All I know was that General Ojdanic came to occupy the post of the Chief of the General Staff and then he became my superior, as Perisic used to be before. I don't know about Perisic's movement from that time on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, it sounds to me that we are talking about the same thing. General Ojdanic took the place of General Perisic. Are you aware, sir, of the position that General Perisic was transferred to and whether in his new position he had any command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you would also have been familiar with Aleksandar Dimitrijevic as well, I take it?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: He was head of the security administration for the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could look at D169, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You'll see here, General Dimitrijevic addressing issues with respect to the border as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we can look at page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'll just actually read this to you and invite your comment, about way down I'll start. He states: "In all aspects, I still firmly" -- and, sir, before I continue, this is from a meeting of the 17th of December, 1998 of the VJ General Staff collegium. He states: "In all aspects, I still firmly support the idea that we, and we have here the most recent reports, that we should deal with things that have been assigned to us by the constitution, the protection of the border." He continues, but if I can just skip ahead somewhat, he says: "So my proposal is, and I've been repeating it week in week out, that all our measures must focus on closing as much of the border as possible, cutting off all their channels and making it impossible for them to import weapons and for people to get in, thereby creating the preconditions for the MUP to resolve other problems, because this is not the army's task." So again, sir, would you agree that what we are seeing are indications that the VJ's proper role was to be acting only within the border area, of course absent any state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia, or rather, the border units were duty-bound to act in the border area and they did so. I cannot remember a particular term and date but it happened very seldom that they intervened in order to pursue terrorist groups. If they would notice them and if they would clash with them then it was their duty to pursue them until they capture them or destroy them. That is what the law prescribes and that was what was done. Most often they would withdraw to the territory of Albania because they had their bases and support there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Following from that, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask something. Although my learned friend Mr. Behar is reading to the witness, the page in Serbian does not correspond to what my friend is reading to him. So he cannot read it for himself. I just wanted to note that. And to check whether I heard this right. Is this D169 or D196? That will be all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That was D169. In fact, I believe there may have been a typo on our initial notification, which might be a source of some confusion. I think, though, if it's convenient for the Chamber, I'll move on. I believe the witness's answer to the question was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The problem may be that the B/C/S page on the screen does not correspond to the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think that's a fair point. I would propose to proceed just in light of the witness's answer, which I think was clear. Although, if he wishes it, we can certainly take a moment to try to find the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, just picking up on what you had said in your last answer, in fact, the VJ forces, as you've indicated, could actually engage in operations when they've been attacked, so in other words, if the VJ were attacked, not just inside the border area, but also outside the border area, then they were legitimately allowed to defend themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not talking about the VJ force. Again, I repeat, I was talking about the border units that were securing the state border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They had the legal right to operate in the border area. Further from the border area, they could act only if they were pursuing fugitives or terrorist groups until they would capture them or hand them over to another organ who would pursue them further. According to the rules, the border units are not supposed to operate outside the border area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. But if we can talk about VJ forces generally, is it not true that, in fact, inside the border area or outside the border area, wherever the VJ happened it to be, they are legitimately allowed to defend themselves if they're attacked?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every man has the right to defend himself if he is under attack. The same goes for a military unit if it is attacked. It is not going to surrender, it is going to defend itself wherever that may happen. That is my personal view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: It's, in fact, not just your personal view, it's pursuant to law, correct? It's well understood that if the VJ operating anywhere is attacked, then of course, they can respond and this is often the reason used to explain why certain action was undertaken?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they have the right to react where and when they are attacked and to prevent those forces from attacking them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we can see P1335, please. If we can have page 15 in the English and page 14 in the B/C/S. And just beginning just underneath where it says: "Colonel-General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic." He states here, sir: "This isn't a question, more a reproach, one for which General Curcin is least to blame. When we take the public line that one of our units, a convoy of soldiers have been attacked, that's okay if one can't do otherwise, but why does the 3rd Army lie to the General Staff?" And he continues, sir, in the next paragraph: "It has been said here that the army has been attacked six times over the past week." I can indicate, as I should have indicated earlier, this document is from 4th of March, 1999. It says: "It has been said here the army has been attacked six times over the past week. Gentlemen, you have to know in this action or operation, as they call it, because they call it an operation, whenever they engage a single platoon ..." He refers to an incident in which a sergeant was killed. Then the next line, sir, he says: "Come now, this was a planned activity by units of the 3rd Army or the Pristina Corps, ordered, carried out, and completed in just the way it was completed." He goes on, sir, but in the interest of time I'll stop there. It seems to me that what General Dimitrijevic is saying there is that the army has in fact been lying about being attacked, when, in fact, they were engaged in planned operations. My question for you is: Was that practice reporting that one was attacked in order to justify offensive operations, was that also prevalent within the border areas?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly have to express my surprise at this kind of statement. As for the activity of the army or any other forces in the territory of Kosovo, I don't know about that. That was not my line of work. I do know one thing, that the army and all forces engaged in the border area never acted unlawfully, and there were no examples of unlawful activity. Now, please, as for statements made by Aleksandar Dimitrijevic, that doesn't mean a thing to me. It would be best to call him to testify in this court and explain his positions taken at the collegium meeting that I'm totally unaware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: In fact, sir, having voiced his dissent in that open way at this meeting, Mr. Dimitrijevic was replaced shortly thereafter, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was replaced. I mean, that is a question for the collegium of the Chief of General Staff, or rather for the Chief of General Staff. If he was replaced, why he was replaced, and if he was not replaced, why he was not replaced. I mean, for me, it doesn't mean a thing because I don't know, I'm not a member of the collegium or of the personnel body that deals with such matters as far as personnel policy is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I don't want to spend too much time on this point, sir, but perhaps we'll have a quick look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 00799.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So this is a document dated the 25th of March. In fact, you can see that the general has been replaced in his position by Geza Farkas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I have to respond by saying that I do not know that he was replaced or relieved of duty because he was being appointed to another position or whether he was retiring. I mean, I relieved of duty when I retired, when I met the requirements for retirement. I see here that this is an order concerning Geza Farkas, but I really don't know whether Dimitrijevic was relieved of duty because he was replaced or because he retired or whatever, I mean, that is not my line of work, and I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for reasons, sir, but you can see from the document that General Dimitrijevic's duty was resumed by Geza Farkas, that much is plain, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, that he was appointed chief of the security administration, Mr. Geza Farkas, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your Honours, I would seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01527.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, we've seen that these are some very powerful people who have expressed direct concerns about the propriety and legality of using a VJ in Kosovo in the absence of state of emergency, and I'll suggest to you once again, sir, that one of the reasons that the border belt was expanded was because the VJ could not otherwise be legally used unless there was a state of emergency declared; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I've already said, and I repeat once again, we expanded the border belt conditionally speaking. It went further in depth into the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in order to create a legal basis for the action of border units in terms of securing the state border within the border area. That is the core of the matter. The lawful use of these units, that was our objective, and we did not want to deviate from the law in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, General Perisic was the highest military ranking member of the VJ or certainly we can agree he was a man of great power and significance holding a high rank. He was the man who made the first legal request to expand the border belt in July of 1998. And he also, as we've seen, could not have been more clear in expressing his view that the VJ could only be lawfully used within the border area. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree that General Perisic had proposed that. He did not propose that. He did not make that request. It was people who deal with the system of securing the state border that proposed that. From the lowest level, the border battalion, up to the service working for the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. My service realised what had to be done because of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, and it proposed that this be discussed by the General Staff. So at that meeting of the collegium of the General Staff where I participated when the border was discussed, I explained these proposals and the border belt was expanded, or rather to put it more precisely, it was established further in depth. Perisic as an individual had nothing whatsoever to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, I think you've told us already, and I don't dispute that people from a lower level may have passed on proposals and certainly would regularly relay information to the General Staff and to General Perisic who was Chief of the General Staff, but, in fact, it was General Perisic who took the decision to move it forward; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the collegium of the Chief of General Staff. That is, the collegium. It was the collegium that made the decision to make this proposal to the government. General Perisic was just Chief of General Staff and head of that collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that you have largely answered that question, sir. Let me move to a very different topic. Sir, in your role, in your employment, beginning in late March of 1999 and for at least the next month, you would have observed literally hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians streaming across the border leaving the country. Let me ask you first, sir, is that something you observed?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me respond. I did not see hundreds of thousands or did I receive such information that Kosovo Albanians were leaving the country. However, it is correct that I did read in the media that a certain number of individuals, a large number of individuals, crossed the border thus leaving the country. Now, whether that information is correct or not, I cannot say. I heard that through the media because the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia under whose jurisdiction crossing the border was, did not have the duty according to the law to inform the General Staff about such developments in the border area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I don't believe that the numbers of people leaving Kosovo, the number of Kosovo Albanians leaving Kosovo is really in dispute in this case, but is it your position then that you did not see these hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians coming across the borders that you were working at?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as for my area of responsibility, that is to say at the state border outside border crossings and built-up areas, it was forbidden to cross the border. If such individuals tried to cross the border, they were returned to report to the appropriate organ of the Ministry of the Interior and to cross the border in a lawful way, where the border crossing is. Probably a certain number of persons crossed the border illegally just like terrorist groups crossed the state border to Albania and Macedonia over those years, and not only then, that is happening now, and that will always be the case at any border. But we did not allow anyone to cross the border, and we returned them to localities where the border could be crossed legally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir, and we already have your evidence where you've been clear that it was the MUP who controlled the border crossings, we are aware of that. All I'm asking you is what you observed, and you've been clear that you were at the borders. What I'm interested in is your observations, you personally.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the crossing of the border is something that did function, that was there, because we caught people who had legally crossed the border coming back illegally and bringing in weapons illegally. I told you that the other day as well. There were such cases, they would legally cross the border and then illegally try to smuggle weapons across the border. The border crossings points were functioning and the population could move legally. The Djeneral Jankovic border post was closest in my area, whereas all the other border posts were in remote mountain areas where people lived and worked and carried out their border duties. It was far away from the border crossing points.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: We can come to the -- a discussion of the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing in a moment, sir. But again, just because I don't think I'm actually getting an answer to my question. I understand that the MUP maintained the border crossing. What I'm asking you is for observations of the hundreds of thousands of people who were pouring through those border crossings while you were working at the border for the VJ. Surely, sir, while you were at the border you would have seen what others have described as miles of tractors, people waiting, massing at the border while they were being processed by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall say once again that I and my people, well, did not inform me about this. There were cases when some state organ official would be at the border crossing and they could unofficially say that there were people crossing the border. But as far as I know, this started en masse once the aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia started in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, and that's in fact what I'm asking about in March. But, sir, if we can look briefly at your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: This is D569. If we could look at paragraph 11. I apologise, I'm not sure the exact page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: We can see, sir, that, in fact, in your own statement you directly state that 837.166 persons left during the time of the war. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Perhaps I have the wrong reference. No, it's there, the second paragraph, in paragraph 11. It's right in the middle of the second paragraph. You see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's para 11, right? I see the first para 11 here. The second paragraph. Yes, towards the Republic of Albania from Kosovo and Metohija. Only during the proclamation of a state of war in the territory of the FRY, 837.166 persons left, et cetera, et cetera. And I underline, this is very important, "I would like to point out that I did not have this information at the time, and I also emphasise that I found this number in media reports just after the NATO aggression. Different media reported different figures. And that's why I stressed my reservation here saying that I did not receive any figures from the MUP but through media reports we found out this number because I thought it important to show what the NATO aggression had done to the population and they were leaving not only towards Albania and other countries, but also to Macedonia and Serbia which were integral parts of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you've relied on that figure, and I don't doubt that you may not have had the precise number down to the one at the time, but having accepted a figure of that size, surely, sir, when you were working at the border, you would have observed every day hundreds or thousands of people streaming across the borders, that's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't seem to want to understand me. My area of work was the border belt, and we acted in the border belt and we didn't -- we were not present at the border watching people cross. 25 kilometres is the length of the border facing Albania. People were deployed there to protect the sovereignty of their state and if somebody just happened to be on the border crossing, they would have been able to see these columns. My job was never at the border crossing, but the people who lived and worked in the forbidding terrain of the Junik mountain and Pastrik mountain et cetera. Again, let me emphasise that this number comes from a media report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Without wishing to interrupt my colleague's examination, I would just like to say that when questions like this are asked, perhaps we should first establish where the witness was at the time in order not to go around in circles. I just don't want to suggest or lead in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I'll admit to feeling some surprise that these significant events at the border didn't garner more attention at the time, at least from what you are describing. But you have addressed, you did in fact, maybe ten minutes ago mention that you were close to the Djeneral Jankovic border. Can you describe for this Court the situation at the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing in late March and early April of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say one thing once again. Sir, please, I did not say I was close to the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing. I said that one of the military installations that watch tower or the border post for accommodation of people was close to the border crossing. I'm really hurt by these insinuations because I said something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I see my friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's precisely my objection. In his evidence the witness never said that he had ever been close to the border crossing, and I just wanted to ask for a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Behar. Don't look back, go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, we've heard quite extensive evidence in this case about what was seen at that border crossing. I'm going to ask you some questions, and you can tell us whether that is something that you either saw yourself or were made aware of at the time. We've heard, sir, about freight train cars that were jammed full of people arriving and unloading at that border crossing. We've heard about large numbers of Kosovo Albanians walking between railway tracks into a no-man's land between the Serbian and Macedonian borders. We've heard about masses of Kosovo Albanians remaining in this area, this no-man's land, often for days until they were removed by bus to refugee camps. I understand, sir, that this was a border crossing and that the specific border crossing was under the control of the MUP. What I'm asking you, sir, is given the significance of those events, how unusual those events would have been, what did you see and what did you know about those events at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: About that event that you are putting to me now, I didn't know and hadn't heard anything at the time. I just read in one report that there were quite a few people who were crossing at Djeneral Jankovic, part of them crossed, and another part of them had been turned back. I never said anything different. I underline again, the purview of the border units was outside border crossings and populated areas in the border belt. And, please, I'd appreciate it if I were asked only questions about the border belt and things that were within my purview. And on those questions, I will always provide correct information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, were you familiar with the practice of the Serb forces taking away identification documents from Kosovo Albanians, and I'm referring specifically here to 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing of it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So your testimony here today, sir, is that up until this very moment, you never heard concerns expressed about Kosovo Albanians having their identity documents taken away from them, either on their way to the border or as they crossed the border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really never heard about that before this day. I never discussed those matters with anyone, and since I was retired, I've never discussed my previous job with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you would certainly agree that identification documents were of great significance to anyone wanting to cross the border; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I can agree with. That is the main document for anyone's movement. You have to prove your identity. It's still so today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, we've heard extensive evidence in this case about identification being taken away from Kosovo Albanians on their way to the border and at the border. So let me ask you just yes or no, did you see identification that had been put into piles, taken away from people and put into piles? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Then I guess you've been clear then, sir, that you've never saw any identification being taken away, certainly not being burned?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen either because I haven't been at a border crossing with Albania for the last ten years. The last time I went to the Albanian border in 1996 when I was going to attend the mixed commission for violations of the border regime, and that was the last time because the Albanian side was no longer willing to convene a meeting of that commission although they had been required to do so by the law. When I was saying goodbye to the Albanians at the Bozaj border crossing that was the last time I was at the Albanian border and at a border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You are also saying this is not a practice that you were made aware of by others given your position?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I wasn't interested in that. I was doing my job, within my competences.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that having your identification destroyed, we can deal with it this hypothetically, having one's identification being taken away and destroyed, would make it virtually impossible and at a bear minimum far more difficult for anyone to regain access to Kosovo, to come back into the country?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think hypothetical questions should be asked here. I came here to tell the truth and nothing but the truth and that's the oath that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question. [Microphone not activated] The Chamber will determine what questions are proper to be put to you, and you will then please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll answer the question, but it's a hypothetical one. If this, then that. I really don't think it's necessary to take away documents. If anyone had ever done that. I think -- I mean, a document is there to prove your identity and that the authorities can see your personal details from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: In fact, sir, if someone showed up at the border with no identification documents and nothing to identify them, they would not be admitted; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so because under the law they would not be allowed to let them cross the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Those are my questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Behar. Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Colonel, when you were answering a question from my learned friend, Mr. Behar, on page 14, I'll para-phrase before I'm able to give you an exact reference. It's lines 9 through 12. The question was: "Bearing in mind the importance of the events on the border, the highest ranking people in the VJ and the MUP had to be informed of what was going on there; is that correct?" And you answered in the affirmative. Now, I want to ask you, do you know about the system of conveying information within the ministry and how it operated?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I wasn't interested. It's a completely different sector, a different method of operation. All I know that within the Army of Yugoslavia, battalion commands were duty-bound to inform the corps, and the corps had to inform the General Staff and in the event of violations on the state border, we insisted that the General Staff be also copied that same document because urgent action was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So this answer that the supreme authorities had to be informed, is it actually your assumption, you don't have any specific knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have specific knowledge, but I know that the General Staff was informed about incidents on the state border, those incidents that were within the competence of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P1526 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's a collegium meeting of the 17th of July. It was much discussed during your evidence and your statement given to the OTP, and I would like to see page 14 in B/C/S. So this is a collegium meeting of 17 July 1998. Colonel, we will look at this last paragraph that you had been asked about. It says: "It is necessary during the day" and you did not emphasise this to the government, "to send a request to expand the border belt facing Macedonia, because it's been widened facing Macedonia from 2.5 to 5 kilometres until the entry into the Sreves [phoen] area." Now, you didn't emphasise this before, but it says here, you did not emphasise this to the federal government to send a request.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A proposal had been sent to the federal government to widen the border belt, and in this case of widening, or rather in the proposal, a specific suggestion was made to widen the border belt facing Albania and partly Macedonia. It was made in one single request.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So on the 17th of July, the federal government had already received it. And it says here you did not emphasise to the federal government.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose contribution is this, who is saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I think General Perisic is speaking here. The Prosecutor asked you about this already. So Perisic is saying this. And we don't have much time. In the next passage, Major-General Smiljanic says, the problem is that the federal government had already approved the widening of the border, so on the 17th of July, the approval of the government already exists apparently, and it is to come into effect on the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise now, but I believe this applies to the prior widening of the border belt when it was widened only facing Albania, not Macedonia. Now we have a new situation, terrorist forces via Macedonia and Sara mountain had already started to smuggle in arms and the need arose to widen the border belt to better protect the border area and put a stop to this terrorist activity. So he probably means the widening only facing Albania, whereas the next widening was both facing Albania and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we are talking about verifiers from the KVM, let us clear up certain matters that I believe remained unclear. Did you issue verifiers with any permits, or were they required to give you notifications?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't have frequent contacts with the authorities of the KVM, only as the need arose. However, verifiers, provided notification of each of their movements. They didn't need any special permits. Once they notify their plan, that automatically means they are allowed to go wherever they like. We only wanted to have that plan to be able to protect these people while they were moving within the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the governing principle of your relationship in 1998 with them?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did anything change in 1999 in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the state of war was proclaimed, nothing. When the state of war was proclaimed, my duties ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, when we are talking about your duties concerning the state border, did they encompass the entire border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia facing all the neighbouring countries?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was chief of the service for the state border of the FRY, and it was my duty in those unfortunate years to monitor the situation along the entire state border, to take appropriate steps along the entire stretch of the border to protect the FRY and its security and integrity vis-a-vis Albania, Hungary, Bulgaria, Romania, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were refugees present at all the borders with all the neighbouring countries and within Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Serbian border, the border between Serbia proper and the autonomous province of Kosovo, there were refugees we could see when we were going on a visit. There were Albanians, and Serbs, and Montenegrins among them. People from all ethnic communities that lived in Kosovo. It was a massive flow of people heading north, or north-west. Of course, I could see that when I visited, when I travelled there.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are now talking about the interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, towards Serbia proper, but also Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Just to be more precise about certain things you said to the Prosecution, did you go to Kosovo and Metohija in 1999 and if so, how many times, and when?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to remember the dates. During the state of war, I travelled to Kosovo because I wanted to go there, to see these people, and quite simply, I travelled there. I had travelled there even before the state of war was proclaimed to check and inspect the system of state border protection and to see what problems are being encountered and what we at the higher level need to do to facilitate the life and work of those people who are directly involved in securing the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that every citizen of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time was recorded in certain registers of births and et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the case even now. It's a lasting document that has been so for centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And if you deprive someone of their ID card, do you erase their identity?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. This is the end of my examination, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The answer was no, the answer it to the previous question was no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me. Okay, we have the answer on the record now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to come back to the number of refugees and crossing the border to Albania and Macedonia. You said -- this is page 60 of today's transcript, line 14 and the following: "I also emphasise that I found this number in media reports just after the NATO aggression. Different media reports different figures. And that's why I stressed my reservation here saying that I did not receive any figures from the MUP but through media reports we found out this number." In your statement of 2007 you said in paragraph 11: "According to reports of the Serbian MUP Ministry of the Interior, during the time of the war alone, 837.166 persons left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija through FRY border crossings in Kosovo and Metohija for the Republic of Albania and the Republic of Macedonia." I'm a little bit astonished about your today's testimony about your source for your information about the number, the very precise number of 837.166 refugees. Could you explain this contradiction?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain. I found that number in one of the media reports, and I just copied it. I don't know what media it was. But I deliberately took it down because that number was given. I didn't say around 800.000 or around 850.000. This is the precise number I found in a media report, and I really did not have any information at the time. I can say that with full responsibility. Neither I nor the General Staff had any information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And why did you say when you were examined by the Defence "according to reports of the Serbian MUP" and mentioned that as your source?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain that now. I said that because this reporter referred to a MUP of Serbia report, and he said in his article according to the reports of the MUP of Serbia, and that's what I repeated. Whether this information is correct, I don't know to this day. I quoted this number because that was in the report, and I expressed my doubts as to the voracity of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Didn't mention the media and that you read this figure in the media when you were asked in the year 2007?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't have any reports at the time from the MUP. Or maybe that is my omission that I didn't state explicitly that it was according to media reports. That may be my mistake. It's my mistake that I did not give a reference to my source of information because I can't remember which medium it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This statement, D569, you gave a precise figure. This morning you said, "different media reports had different figures." Why did you say in 2007 and reported specific number of refugees?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that was a specific piece of information. Everybody said approximately, whereas this was a specific figure. A specific number. I thought that it may have been the case that they had this exact figure. They didn't say around 800, around 500 or whatever, they gave a very specific figure so I thought that that might have been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That completes the questions for you. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance and for the assistance you have been able to give, and you may return to your normal activities now and after we rise, a Court Officer will show you out. We now adjourn to resume at 1.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to raise a question very briefly before the next witness enters the courtroom. It has to do with witness Gojovic who testified before this Trial Chamber. On that occasion, on behalf of the Defence in relation to one of the documents that was admitted during his testimony, I took it upon myself to make certain corrections in document D510 and to submit these corrections both to our colleagues from the Prosecution and to you as the Trial Chamber. In the meantime, I discussed that with Ms. Gopalan who cross-examined that witness. My colleagues from the OTP tell me that she is not here at the moment, but I would like to inform the Chamber that we did act upon the obligation we took, and we refer to a part of the transcript which is our basis for tendering the document with all its pages. It is uploaded in e-court and right now -- and it is registered as 0112257 in B/C/S and D001-2128 in English. If the Chamber believes that we need to wait for the response of the OTP, of course we can do so, but I would just like to tell you that we did act as instructed by you and we have made sure that you received this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I think we ought, as a matter of courtesy, to wait until Ms. Gopalan can just confirm the position she takes. So if you could arrange a time when she is here to bring that up or else be in a position to communicate her comments when you raise it next. Thank you, Mr. Popovic. The next witness? Is this you, Mr. Popovic, or -- you are handing over to wiser people, are you, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I will agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I see Ms. Kravetz and Ms. Petersen. Which way should I look? Ms. Petersen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Popovic. I was distracted by which was the wiser.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe. Who knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Radoicic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put some questions to you today in relation to matters that are important for the Djordjevic Defence. Since we speak the same language, I will ask you to be careful to wait for me to finish the question that I'm putting to you so that the interpreters have enough time to interpret that to all of those who do not speak or understand our language. So please give your answer only after that. I am doing this because we have this problem practically on a regular basis. Even I, who has been appearing before this Court for over two years, still seem to have this problem, so I will kindly ask you to focus.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please give me your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Milan Radoicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: In Sietinja [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of March, 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now briefly tell all in this courtroom what this witness is going to testify about today and probably for part of tomorrow. He will testify about paragraphs 1 to 5 and 16 to 23 of the indictment. He was chief of the office of the commander of the 1st Army from 1994 until the end of 1998 until he was appointed deputy chief of office of the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army. He will explain to us what the main duties were of the head of office of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. While carrying out these duties, it was indispensable to co-ordinate all planned, special, and other tasks that were confirmed by the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. In that period, the Chief of General Staff was directly subordinated to the president of the Republic of Yugoslavia who at the same time was commander of the VSO. As such, the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia had the duty, meaning the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, to prepare all documents and in co-operation with professional relevant elements, sectors, independent departments, and other organisational units of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and for the military office of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia also compiled monthly and weekly plans of work depending on the annual plan for the work of the Army of Yugoslavia, as well as monthly and daily tasks -- weekly tasks that were set during the collegium of the General Staff -- of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. The witness will also confirm that he co-operated on a daily basis with the Colonel Vlajkovic in writing and formulating tasks after the evening briefings and their technical processing and distribution to appropriate organisational units of the staff and the Supreme Command and other state organs if that was required. The witness will explain how the minutes from the meetings of the collegium of the Supreme Command staff were technically processed and what individuals he did that with. All the transcripts minutes were kept. The witness will also explain the distribution of official communications at the relevant office. He will also explain his attendance at the collegium and also he will say that he was present several times at these meetings when in the evenings, the situation in the theatre of war was discussed. He will confirm that he has no information about the ethnic cleansing of Albanians in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radoicic, I would now like to ask you to tell us all where you went to school and which schools you completed. So please tell us about your schooling from the very beginning up until the moment when you --

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear the last bit you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I wanted to ask you whether you gave a statement on the 17th of August, 2007, to the investigators -- to investigators Ratko Djukanovic and Ilija Isic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today, would you repeat everything that you said then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That statement is marked as D010-0746, and I would like to have it admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00581.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radoicic, did you testify before this Court in the case of Milutinovic et al.?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you same things then that you said -- today that you said then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The transcript is marked D010-3903, and I would like to tender the transcript from Milutinovic et al., please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00582, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back now to the questions that I started putting to you at a very early stage. Please tell me which schools you completed and when, so I don't want to interrupt you, I'm not going to put any additional questions, let's try to be as efficient as possible so you please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I completed elementary and secondary school in Podgorica, which was then called Titograd in Montenegro which was then part of a Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I completed the military economic academy in Belgrade. Later on while I was working, I studied law part time, and I ultimately received a master's degree at the Faculty of Law in Osjek in Zagreb. Towards the end of my career, I received a doctorate and that completes my education. That is what I had to say about my education.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you to describe to us your professional career. Was your first job in the military, or did you actually ever work outside the military, that's a separate question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Immediately upon completing the military economic academy according to the system that was in place then and the regulations that were in place then, it was my duty to get employment with the Yugoslav People's Army. That involved inter alia that I was prepared to be transferred anywhere in the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. My first post was in Senta at the north, and later on my professional duties took me throughout the territory of Yugoslavia. Towards the end of my career, I resided in Belgrade and up until the end of my career, I was in Belgrade for the most part. As for the duties I had when I arrived in Belgrade and after I got my degree in law was head of the office of the commander of the 1st Army, as you already said. That was from 1994, and then up until the end of my career, I held positions that were at that level but in different institutions from the level of the office of the commander of the army up to the minister of defence. So it was the commander of the 1st Army then of the Yugoslav People's Army, later on the VJ, the Army of Yugoslavia, then the deputy head of office of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, then the chief of office of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. And towards the end of my career I was head of office of the federal defence minister, when it was the federal defence minister and finally of the minister of defence of Yugoslavia. So Serbia and Montenegro was when my career ended on the 14th of April, 2003. On that occasion Mr. Boris Tadic was minister of defence. He is now president of Serbia. That would be my career in the briefest possible terms, and those were the jobs I held as a professional member of the Army of Yugoslavia, the JNA, and finally the Army of Serbia. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you decorated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your retirement, was it regular?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes, the procedure was completely regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, which post did you occupy during the NATO attack against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia until the end of that conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: At that time I was officially deputy chief of office of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and in the period from the beginning of the aggression until the end of the aggression, I was deputy chief of office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. To laymen, this may sound like the same thing, but there is a subtle difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I needed a clarification of that myself while I was proofing you. What is the difference between the General Staff in peacetime, that's how the institution was called, and the Supreme Command staff, and while you are explaining that, compare your duties in peacetime with those in war time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: In peacetime, the armed forces have at the top of the pyramid because there is a system of subordination that looks like a pyramid, and at the top of that pyramid there was the General Staff of the armed forces. It used to be in the past the General Staff of the JNA, but with the constitutional amendments and the changes in Yugoslavia, the latest organisational form was the General Staff of the armed forces. At that time I was deputy chief of office of the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ. Under the circumstances that everyone is well aware of during the aggression, the entire defence system, everything that is stipulated by the defence law as opposed to the Law on the Army, we all functioned in keeping with that law. But with the proclamation of the state of war, the entire defence system, in addition to armed forces, integrated all the other available parts of the defence system so that the General Staff switched from its peacetime function to the Supreme Command staff, expanding its duties. It's not easy to compare the functions in peacetime with a system of defence governed by the Supreme Command staff in war. The duties multiplied. The Supreme Command staff is a much more complex institution compared to the General Staff of the VJ. You cannot really compare these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What did that mean in terms of your duties? There were duties you performed while there was General Staff of the armed forces. What did you do when you became part of the Supreme Command staff? What did that mean for you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, for me and all those who were involved, it meant that our duties multiplied to a high degree, and it was completely impossible to predict what the war was going to bring, and it was a big question whether we would be able to meet the requirements of the new situation. It's very difficult to explain this briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Would you now describe your personal involvement in the days when you were at the Supreme Command staff. For instance, did you have working hours? If so, what were they, what were your duties, how did you organise yourself at the time. And a third question within this one, did anyone stand in for you when you had to rest or be absent for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: We were all aware that this was a situation when our engagement had to extend beyond our real physical abilities and the number of our duties multiplied by the day, and even by the hour. And we had to deal with it by carrying out our assignments. Everything else was on a back burner including our normal rest. No one even gave it any thought. If the Chief of the Supreme Command staff and his man number two were involved in that way, care had also be taken to avoid complete exhaustion of the personnel. So every day we were concerned how long we could keep this up, and we made something that looked like a plan, including a plan for replaceability or interchangeability, including for me and Mr. Stojiljkovic [as interpreted], in view of the duties that were multiplying constantly. And this monitoring by our superiors and these plans kept us from coming to a point where every individual would be completely exhausted, but we were certainly exerting ourselves to the limit. There were no normal working hours, and in the 72 days that the bombing lasted, we worked from morning until dawn because we knew that the way we tackled our obligations could either lead to a successful outcome or to grave consequences that we couldn't even foresee.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to intervene. I'm sorry if I misheard, but on page 82, line 4, I see the name Stojiljkovic. Did you say Stojilkovic or Vlajkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: It must be an error, because I said Vlajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 82, line 4, should be Vlajkovic instead of Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that. Although I hadn't paid attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never mind, it's just a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but even in line -- oh, no, no, sorry, that's your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's my correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, would you please try in the form of narrative to describe what specifically you did on your job at that time, when I say that time, I mean for the duration of the war. You were in the office of the Chief of the General Staff as deputy to Mr. Vlajkovic. We want to know what you were doing, what Mr. Vlajkovic was doing, what your obligations were, was there anything different in the way you carried out these duties, and if so, what were the differences?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I think there's one thing you should focus on one thing -- I'm sorry, okay. There are running corrections to the transcript. You mentioned the General Staff. At that time it was no longer the General Staff, it was the Supreme Command staff. And I was deputy chief of office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. I emphasise this because I said before, it's almost impossible to compare the duties of the General Staff with those of the Supreme Command staff. And I would suggest to you to pay attention to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radoicic, it was my mistake this time. I meant the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, the entire office and the entire Supreme Command staff were at that time at a certain location in a facility that had much earlier in peacetime been prepared for unhindered work of the Supreme Command staff in emergencies, like the one that actually occurred. It was designed to serve that purpose, it was specially built, and it did indeed serve the purpose completely. There were certain restrictions, of course, because it's a different feeling to be working underground, and some people suffered from claustrophobia, that's the feeling you get when for prolonged periods of time you cannot get fresh air or air the room or open a window. And working under those circumstances and the feeling that you were underground was one of the factors that created some sort of psychological resistance in some people. Those were the objective circumstances. Now, as far as I'm concerned, in view of the situation in the country and the fact that an extraordinary situation, a state of emergency had been proclaimed, everything was an emergency and that affected the numbers and the character of our work. The people, the number of people who served the General Staff in peacetime, and the number of people serving on the Supreme Command staff were the same. The numbers did not increase for some reasons unknown to me. Probably because there was a need to deploy people in an optimal way. And Mr. Vlajkovic as chief of the office and me as his deputy saw our duties multiplied, which meant that we had to invest a lot more effort and that in its turn caused a great strain. However, two or three days later when we had already adjusted to some extent to the extraordinary duties we were performing, we tried to make some sort of plan to achieve an optimum deployment of our resources and personnel, but I also have to emphasise that in addition to those tasks that were expected, unexpected tasks occurred every day. Mr. Vlajkovic and I no longer really worried much about what were strictly his duties and what were mine. We had a normal co-operation on a human level, and we adjusted by the hour to ensure the best possible work of the Supreme Command staff, and our job descriptions extended and expanded all the time in view of what was going on in the territory of our entire country. Except for the chief of the Supreme Command staff, we needed to meet the requirements of all the other agencies that the Supreme Command staff was working with, including strategic groups on the ground, and in the work-place of the Supreme Command staff itself, which involved also the president of the Supreme Defence Council, who was then the president of the country, so the Chief of the Supreme Command staff had very complex duties at the time, and his office had to support him fully at all times and provide proposals for all the tasks that he had to deal with. In addition to those regular duties, the office had on a daily basis to maintain direct communication with all the units and commands including the strategic groups, that means the 1st Army, 2nd Army, 3rd Army commands, air defence, and air force navy, federal authorities, federal government, et cetera. It's a whole range of communications wherein the chief of the office had to function efficiently with full responsibility, and those were his requirements and our responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since my next question will require an answer not less than 15 minutes long, preferably uninterrupted, I suggest that we adjourn a minute earlier and continue tomorrow. It would be wiser, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now and resume tomorrow and continue the evidence of the witness then. So we adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Court Officer will assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
